fix.shows: Nishtha Gupta, a technology policy researcher based in New Delhi, argues that the revision replaced the presumption the Supreme Court set out in 1995, that a name already on the roll is there lawfully, with data matching by software. She describes rolls from the last intensive revision, mostly of 2002, digitised and transliterated into English by machine and then matched against the new enumeration forms, followed by tests for logical discrepancies such as a parent and child less than 15 years apart. By her account those who failed these tests included twins, Oraon voters whose surname Xalxo was rendered as Khalkho, and voters whose father's name was Md. in one list and Mohammed in the other, and according to the Internet Freedom Foundation the rules flagged 17% of West Bengal's electors and 41% of Madhya Pradesh's. She cites 91% of decided exclusion appeals in West Bengal going in the appellant's favour, 728 of 729 voters cut at one booth in Delhi's Bela Estate, and about 200 notices for each booth level officer in Delhi to verify within a very tight deadline. She asks the Commission to publish its matching rules and error rates, to open itself to an independent audit, and to delete no name until an officer with the time and authority has verified the person behind the record.
fix.note: The online page (published 28 October 2026, 1:06 am IST, updated 1:07 am, Comment section, by Nishtha Gupta) serves the first two paragraphs and then asks the reader to register, so it is marked as needing a subscription or sign-in. The rest was read from the printed op-ed page of 28 October 2026, Chennai edition, as supplied by the owner, which carries the full text and the byline 'Technology policy researcher based in New Delhi'. Every figure in the summary is the author's. The 13 crore she calls removed are the names left off the drafts, 13,39,03,307 in 31 states (data/india/states.json), where dead and duplicate entries are 28.5% and shifted, absent or other 71.5%, which agrees with her 'over a quarter' dead or duplicated and 'most' absent or shifted. Her 17% and 41% are in the Internet Freedom Foundation's explainer of 25 September 2026 on the software of the SIR, already on the reading list, which gives 1.31 crore electors flagged in West Bengal (17.11%) and 2.35 crore in Madhya Pradesh (41.22%) and takes them from The Reporters' Collective. Her 91% for West Bengal appeals agrees with the 91.13% the Internet Freedom Foundation took from an RTI reply, and differs from the 93% in the Congress graphic reported by The Hindu on 27 October. No tribunal figures were found to check either against. The 1995 judgment is not named in the piece. The Goa case of 97 electors found eligible whom the software could not restore matches The Indian Express's reporting already on the reading list (its video of 23 September and its report of 27 October on the Commission's affidavit).
